about: Guided tours: each step moves the timeline and the map, highlights a state (a key in public/data/polities.json) and narrates. Text only states what the linked Wikipedia article supports; uncertain dates are hedged with c.

tours.title: The rise of the Zulu
tours.summary: From Nguni chiefdoms to Shaka's kingdom, the Mfecane and the Anglo-Zulu War, c. 1790–1879.

steps.title: Nguni chiefdoms
steps.text: In the late 18th century the land between the Drakensberg and the Indian Ocean was divided among Nguni chiefdoms. The Mthethwa under Dingiswayo and the Ndwandwe under Zwide became the strongest of them.

steps.title: Shaka takes power
steps.text: Shaka, who had risen as a commander in Dingiswayo's army, took over the small Zulu chiefdom c. 1816 with Mthethwa backing and reorganised its fighting men.

steps.title: War with the Ndwandwe
steps.text: After Zwide's Ndwandwe killed Dingiswayo (c. 1817–18), Shaka fought them at Gqokli Hill and defeated them at the Mhlatuze River c. 1819, absorbing the Mthethwa and much of the region.

steps.title: The Mfecane
steps.text: The wars of these years, remembered as the Mfecane, uprooted peoples across southern Africa. Mzilikazi, one of Shaka's commanders, broke away c. 1822–23 and led his followers north; they went on to found the Ndebele kingdom.

steps.title: Shaka's death
steps.text: Shaka was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana, and Dingane became king.

steps.title: Blood River
steps.text: Voortrekkers who had crossed the Drakensberg came into conflict with Dingane. On 16 December 1838 his army was defeated at the Ncome, or Blood River.

steps.title: Mpande and Natal
steps.text: Dingane's half-brother Mpande, allied with the Boers, overthrew him in 1840 and reigned until 1872. To the south the Boer republic of Natalia was annexed by Britain in 1843.

steps.title: The Anglo-Zulu War
steps.text: British forces invaded in January 1879. King Cetshwayo's army won at Isandlwana but was defeated at Ulundi in July, and the kingdom was broken up into thirteen chiefdoms.

tours.title: Polynesian voyaging
tours.summary: How seafarers settled the Pacific, from the Lapita culture to Aotearoa and Rēkohu, c. 1500 BCE–1778 CE.

steps.title: The Lapita culture
steps.text: Around 1500 BCE a pottery-making culture now called Lapita appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago, carried by descendants of Austronesian seafarers from Island Southeast Asia.

steps.title: Into Remote Oceania
steps.text: Within a few centuries Lapita voyagers crossed open sea to Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, and by c. 800 BCE reached Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture took shape.

steps.title: East Polynesia
steps.text: After a long pause, voyagers pushed east to the Society and Cook Islands. Recent radiocarbon studies place the settlement of East Polynesia c. 1000–1200 CE.

steps.title: Hawaiʻi
steps.text: Hawaiʻi was settled from East Polynesia, probably between c. 1000 and 1200 CE.

steps.title: Rapa Nui
steps.text: Rapa Nui, one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth, was settled c. 1200 CE.

steps.title: The Tuʻi Tonga
steps.text: In western Polynesia the Tuʻi Tonga line led a maritime chiefdom whose influence reached Samoa, ʻUvea and beyond, at its height c. 13th century.

steps.title: Aotearoa
steps.text: New Zealand, the last large land mass to be settled, was reached by Polynesian voyagers c. 1250–1300. Their descendants are the Māori.

steps.title: Rēkohu
steps.text: The Chatham Islands, Rēkohu, were settled from New Zealand c. 1500; their people became the Moriori.

steps.title: Contact
steps.text: European ships crossed the Pacific in the 18th century; James Cook, who had sailed with the Raiatean navigator Tupaia in 1769, reached Hawaiʻi in 1778.

tours.title: Mali and Songhai
tours.summary: The great empires of the western Sahel, from Ghana to Mali's golden age and Songhai's fall at Tondibi, c. 1000–1591.

steps.title: The Ghana Empire
steps.text: Before Mali, the Ghana Empire (Wagadu), with its capital at Koumbi Saleh, controlled the trade between the West African goldfields and the trans-Saharan routes.

steps.title: Sundiata and Kirina
steps.text: According to the oral epic of Sundiata, Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina c. 1235 and founded the Mali Empire.

steps.title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
steps.text: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–25, with a famous display of gold in Cairo, made Mali known across the Mediterranean world.

steps.title: Timbuktu
steps.text: Timbuktu and Djenné grew into centres of trade and Islamic scholarship; Timbuktu's Djinguereber Mosque dates from c. 1327.

steps.title: Sonni Ali
steps.text: As Mali weakened, Songhai, centred on Gao, expanded under Sonni Ali (r. c. 1464–1492), who took Timbuktu in 1468.

steps.title: The Askias
steps.text: Askia Muhammad seized power in 1493. Under the Askia dynasty Songhai became one of the largest states in African history.

steps.title: Tondibi
steps.text: A Moroccan army sent by the Saadi sultan Ahmad al-Mansur crossed the Sahara with firearms and defeated Songhai at Tondibi in 1591; the empire broke apart.

tours.title: The Mongol Empire
tours.summary: From rival steppe tribes to the largest contiguous land empire in history and its division, c. 1190–1300.

steps.title: The steppe before Genghis
steps.text: Around 1190 the eastern steppe was divided among rival confederations: the Keraites, Naimans, Merkits, Tatars and the Khamag Mongol of the young Temüjin.

steps.title: Genghis Khan
steps.text: In 1206 an assembly of the united tribes proclaimed Temüjin Genghis Khan.

steps.title: Khwarazm
steps.text: After a Mongol trade caravan was massacred at Otrar, Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarazmian Empire (1219–1221), sacking Bukhara, Samarkand and Urgench.
steps.wikipedia: Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

steps.title: Into Europe
steps.text: Under Batu and Subutai the Mongols conquered the Rus' principalities (1237–1240) and in 1241 defeated Polish and Hungarian armies at Legnica and Mohi.

steps.title: Baghdad
steps.text: Hülegü's army sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate there. In 1260 the Mamluks halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut.

steps.title: Kublai and the Yuan
steps.text: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279.

steps.title: Four khanates
steps.text: By c. 1300 the empire had divided into the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan, which acknowledged the great khan only loosely.

tours.title: Rome: republic, empire and Byzantium
tours.summary: From the Republic to Augustus, the empire's greatest extent, the fall of the West and of Constantinople, 509 BCE–1453 CE.

steps.title: The Republic
steps.text: By tradition Rome expelled its last king in 509 BCE and became a republic, governed by elected magistrates and the Senate.

steps.title: The Punic Wars
steps.text: Rome's wars with Carthage (264–146 BCE) made it the dominant power of the western Mediterranean.

steps.title: Augustus
steps.text: After decades of civil war, Octavian became the first emperor and took the name Augustus in 27 BCE.

steps.title: Greatest extent
steps.text: Under Trajan, who died in 117, the empire reached its greatest extent, from Britain to Mesopotamia.

steps.title: East and West
steps.text: When Theodosius I died in 395 the empire was divided for good between his sons, into eastern and western halves.

steps.title: The end in the West
steps.text: In 476 Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last western emperor; the year is traditionally taken as the fall of the Western Roman Empire. The map shows the West in its final year.
steps.wikipedia: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

steps.title: Justinian
steps.text: The eastern empire endured. Justinian I (r. 527–565) reconquered Italy, North Africa and part of Spain.

steps.title: Constantinople falls
steps.text: The eastern empire, now called Byzantine, shrank over the following centuries; Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
